In the gatehouse of the Shanghai Normal College, Yanzhi came face to face with the man for whom she would throw everything away. Qin Shuji, in a white pointed-collar undershirt, stood dumbstruck a good while before he said, “I still have a class to teach.”
“I'll wait,” Yanzhi said.

Qin Shuji glanced at the campus and the road beyond the gate, took up the cane case, and led her off to a hotel. They crossed a road thick with French plane trees, and the whole way neither knew what to say; the two of them walked like a teacher leading his pupil. Yanzhi could not understand why they were going to a hotel and not to his home. Qin Shuji shut the door and gathered her into his arms. “I want to go to your home,” Yanzhi said.

Qin Shuji spared no breath for talk; it was as it had been that summer at the Xietang inn — a man uses action in place of words, and action too to master his woman, and only afterward lies quiet and thinks with his head. When it was over Qin Shuji looked at her. “You shouldn't have come,” he said.
“Not come?” Yanzhi said. “Then I'd have married my elder apprentice-brother.”
“Now is not the time to come,” Qin Shuji said.
Yanzhi sat bolt upright, the sweat on her body one oily sheen. “What is that supposed to mean?” she said, loudly.

Qin Shuji pressed her back down and stopped her mouth with a kiss. The night deepened with the rise and fall of them, and then Qin Shuji dressed and took her out to eat. All through the meal he was lost in thought, studying the woman before him in the dim light.
Yanzhi raised her head all at once. “Don't tell me you've got a wife,” she said.
Qin Shuji said nothing, and Yanzhi's heart dropped in one plunge, as if it had gone into the river; she felt she could not breathe.

Mrs. Qin was a quiet, gentle woman. It was already autumn when Yanzhi met her. She caught Yanzhi's hand like a sister not seen in years, looked her up and down, and said, pleased, “You really are lovely. No wonder he never wants to come home, day or night.”

This was Qin Shuji's home, in the staff quarters of the Shanghai Art Academy. He was the youngest teacher in the oil-painting department, a master of color and line and form, yet before the two women he sat as mute as a withdrawn child. What Yanzhi found strange was herself: why did she feel nothing at all? Anger, grievance, jealousy, even hurt or humiliation — of all of it Yanzhi felt not a trace. She ate her supper as though at a relative's house. Afterward Mrs. Qin even made three cups of coffee, and the two women sat facing each other and talked of clothes, of hair, of the cosmetics at the Sincere Company.
It was when Yanzhi made to leave that Mrs. Qin caught her by the arm. “Where would you go?” she said. “It's past curfew by now.”
Outside the window, police cars went by now and then with their sirens crying, near and then far. It was a sound to make the heart draw tight.
“Stay the night,” Mrs. Qin said again. “Treat it as your own home.”

Yanzhi's eyes went wide, but Mrs. Qin's smile was so warm, so untroubled; she turned and pulled open a cabinet and set busily about laying out wash-things for her. Yanzhi turned her eyes slowly to Qin Shuji. He stood at the window, gazing out at the street from behind the curtain, rapt. Almost the whole evening he stood like that behind the curtain, as though down on the road below there waited another person who held his heart tighter still.

It was a wretched and thrilling night. Yanzhi shut herself in the bathroom a long while before she came out in Mrs. Qin's nightclothes. Mrs. Qin already lay on one side of the great bed; she looked at her and smiled and patted the pillow beside her. Yanzhi lay down without a sound, and neither of them spoke again. The two women lay side by side, still under the quilt, like two stiffened female corpses in a mortuary. In the small hours Yanzhi rose suddenly in the dark and slipped into Qin Shuji's bedding on the floor. She was fevered then, and past all holding back...

Every day on Jing'an Temple Road was as quiet as a virgin. There Qin Shuji had rented Yanzhi an apartment, but the nights he stayed grew fewer and fewer, and each time he came and went in haste, leaving behind his ardor and that look of something held back and unsaid.
One afternoon Yanzhi said, out of nowhere, “When you've tired of me, I can go.”
Qin Shuji held her tight and put his lips to her ear, and only after a long while said, “I have to earn money. I have to keep this household going.”
“Is it your household?” Yanzhi tilted her face up in his arms and looked straight at him.
Qin Shuji gave a hard nod. “It is,” he said.
Yanzhi worked slowly free of his arms and turned away, holding herself, as loneliness and grief drove all at once into the marrow of her.

Men are all like this. The one who said it was Miss Lin, next door. She was the kept woman of a manager at the Dadong trading house, and while they were having their hair done she told Yanzhi that if you couldn't hold a man's heart you should hold tight to his purse. Yanzhi said she didn't want money; besides, Qin Shuji was no rich man. Miss Lin curled her lip and turned her face away, done with looking at her, and let her eyes throw down a parting line: what's a whore doing raising a chastity arch?

That very night, the moment she saw Qin Shuji at the Western restaurant, Yanzhi said it flat out — she would not live there, she would not live in one building with all those concubines and second wives, and she would not have him wearing himself out to earn money for her.
Qin Shuji nodded. “There's some business at the gallery these few days,” he said. “Let's talk of it once the rush is past.”

Besides teaching at the Shanghai Art Academy, Qin Shuji kept a picture gallery on Fourth Avenue with a friend. Yanzhi had been to that gallery and had met the friend called Ah Si, a plump, pale, middle-aged man in spectacles, all geniality when he laughed. That time she had gone to carry a message for Qin Shuji: that Mr. Liu would not part with his painting after all. Yanzhi saw the smile vanish for an instant from Ah Si's face and could not help thinking the deal must matter to them a great deal. That night, before the steak was even finished, Qin Shuji took her by the arm and would have her dancing at the Paramount, and it was deep in the night before they got back to the apartment on Jing'an Temple Road. Qin Shuji caught her up the moment he was through the door, so urgent, so unquiet.

It was a somewhat strange night. They made love for their lives, as if parting forever. Yanzhi hooked her whole body onto him, as though swinging from a trapeze. Adrift in it she whispered, I mean to hold you fast like this, to the death. But the moment it was out she thought of his wife, as if that quiet, gentle woman were watching them now, silent in the dark. Yanzhi felt it every time, always that pair of eyes in the dark, and it left her at once aroused and cast down.

The next morning Qin Shuji did not hurry off as he always did. Dressed and ready, he sat down at the edge of the bed and gently lifted the quilt from Yanzhi's body, letting it show in the faint dawn, and looked at her rapt, as though admiring his own work. Yanzhi lay still on her side until she heard his long, deep breathing, then could not help turning over, and smiled, and opened her arms. Qin Shuji started, then gathered her in, quilt and all, and said, apologetic, there's no time, I have to go.

After that morning Qin Shuji vanished like dew. Yanzhi knew nothing of it. She went to the department store and bought one jin of wool, and when she had finished knitting Qin Shuji a scarf she bought two jin more and set about knitting him a sweater. It was just then that Ah Si, the gallery's owner, paid a call — the first visitor she had ever had there. All at once Yanzhi had a foreboding, but she dared not dwell on it, and only stared at him dully. Ah Si hesitated, said nothing, drew out thirty silver dollars and laid them on the table, then covered his mouth, coughed twice, and turned to go.
“Wait,” Yanzhi said.
“No need, no need.” Ah Si waved his hands over and over and left as if in flight.

Yanzhi threw a sweater over her shoulders and rushed downstairs. She took a rickshaw to the Shanghai Art Academy, and another rickshaw to the Academy's dormitory. In the end she went the whole way on her own two legs, to the gallery on Fourth Avenue. These were the only three places she knew that had anything to do with Qin Shuji. But the gallery's front door bore a seal of the Shanghai Garrison Command, and so did the door of Qin Shuji's dormitory. At the Academy gate the porter only shook his head and said, again and again, three words: I don't know.

Three months later, when the landlord came a third time to dun her for the rent, Yanzhi decided to go home. She packed her things into the wisteria-cane case and left still more behind in the room. Last of all she took down from the wall a portrait of herself and laid it on top in the case. It was the one Qin Shuji had painted, standing on the far bank of the river the day they first met. Yanzhi had sat at the back window of her family's shop, gazing rapt at this man who painted. It was the first time she had ever known herself to be so beautiful, and so at peace.
